« Avant, nous étions perçus comme des vo: “Before, we were seen as job thieves. Now I’m glad people appreciate us for who we are and the work we do,” Carlos tells me when I reach him around 10 p.m., after his 14-hour shift. “It’s true that we need this work to feed our families, but here they really need us too. It’s a win-win situation.” Foreign agricultural workers show great courage and endurance, motivated mainly by the need to provide for their families. That is why more than 2,500 farmers in Quebec alone are vying for them. The fact that fewer of them are returning this year because of the pandemic has a direct impact on the environment and conditions they are forced to work in.
Carlos fait partie du Programme des trav: Carlos has been part of the Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program (SAWP) for nine years. For the past two years, he has worked the first months of the season at a plant nursery in the Montérégie, then continued until the fall at a vegetable grower in the region. The father of three, originally from Mexico City, first worked in Ontario before starting on market-garden farms in Quebec. After the birth of his first child, he decided to follow in his father’s footsteps and become, like him, a seasonal agricultural worker. “For the first time in 22 years, my father won’t be able to come this year,” says Carlos. Thousands of Mexican workers will be absent this year because of administrative delays in processing their work permits. Carlos is saddened by it: “It’s sad, because we all want to come back to work so we can improve our family’s quality of life.”
Le salaire minimum se situant autour de: With the minimum wage currently around eight dollars a day in Mexico, it would be hard for Carlos to provide for his wife and children, even working overtime. “By working three-quarters of the year here, I can offer my family much more than if I worked at the sawmill all year.” Having arrived in Quebec in February, Carlos has seen his workload increase in recent weeks because several of his colleagues are missing. “Normally, there are 12 Mexican workers at my employer’s, but this year there are only 7.”
En raison de la pénurie de main-d’œuvre: Because of the labour shortage in the middle of the peak perennial season, he starts his shifts at 7 a.m. without knowing what time he will finish. “Sometimes we finish at 6 p.m., other times at 8 or 9 p.m., like today,” he says. “But I’m still happy to be here, despite how intense the work is right now. It’s easier to endure shifts that long in horticulture, since the tasks are less gruelling than in the fields.” Working from morning until very late at night, Carlos often has to plan to bring enough food from home to eat two meals at his workplace. But when his shift is extended on the same day, he is forced to wait before going home for supper.
Sans masque ni gants, Carlos ne se sent: Without a mask or gloves, Carlos doesn’t feel protected from COVID-19 by his employer. “Yet we’ve heard that colleagues on other farms have to wear masks at all times at work,” he notes. Carlos and his colleagues do their best to maintain physical distancing, both at work and in the apartment where their employer houses them, but they face constraints. “Seven of us travel together in a minivan to get to the farm, to go home after work, to go to the grocery store or the bank. Four of us live together, but the other three live elsewhere.”
Joint au téléphone cette semaine, le coo: Reached by phone this week, Michel Pilon, coordinator of the Réseau d’aide aux travailleuses et travailleurs migrants agricoles du Québec (RATTMAQ), says: “We’ve received more than twenty calls from workers who report having been forced to work up to 18 hours a day, and two complaints about workers who were even forced to work during their quarantine period. They would like things to slow down a bit; they’re really exhausted. I think we’re burning the workers out, and there are going to be workplace accidents somewhere if this continues.”
L’Union des producteurs agricoles (UPA): The Union des producteurs agricoles (UPA) had to step in in these cases to remind farmers not to make their employees work more than 12 hours a day. “We keep the complaints anonymous, we don’t give out the workers’ names so they don’t face reprisals,” he continues.
Concernant le port de masques et de gant: His organization has also received a few complaints about the wearing of masks and gloves. “I explain to workers that wearing a mask is mandatory when there are less than two metres between them, and that the employer must provide the necessary protective equipment.” Mr. Pilon says he passed these complaints on to the Commission des normes, de l’équité, de la santé et de la sécurité du travail (CNESST), which is responsible for following up to ensure employers comply with public health rules.
D’après M. Pilon, certains employeurs co: According to Mr. Pilon, some employers are currently confining workers to the farm once their shift is over, an issue he says he raised with the Commission des droits de la personne.
« Il y a des travailleurs qui ont eu des: “Some workers have faced disciplinary measures because they left the farm on their day off,” he says. “Employers say they don’t want COVID-19 to get onto the farm, but when Quebecers come to work on their farms this summer, they won’t be able to confine them there. If they want to go out for a walk after work, they have the right to do so. So why deny that right to the workers? The rules and freedoms must apply in the same way. You can’t treat a temporary worker differently from a Quebecer. That’s discrimination.”
Pilon et son équipe continueront le trav: Pilon and his team will continue their fieldwork until July, to keep handing out Spanish-language pamphlets on COVID-19 and their rights during quarantine to all workers arriving at the Montréal airport.
« Nous ne pourrons pas nourrir les Canad: “We will not be able to feed Canadians at an affordable price without immigrants,” federal Immigration Minister Marco Mendicino said last week when announcing the Liberals’ immigration plan. “We have to ask ourselves at whose expense we can feed ourselves at an affordable price,” Viviana Medina, coordinator at the Immigrant Workers Centre (IWC), fires back at Minister Mendicino. She denounces an inequality that has been intensified by the current pandemic. Viviana Medina argues that the spotlight on the inequalities faced by essential workers should be a wake-up call for all of society. “Now that we realize the machine isn’t working, we have to sit down and think about how we’re going to change things for the most vulnerable people on the front lines right now.”
Près de 16 000 travailleurs agricoles sa: Nearly 16,000 seasonal agricultural workers leave their families in Mexico and Guatemala for a few months each year to come work in Quebec, sometimes for more than two decades, without having the right to settle here. The new Agri-Food Pilot put in place by the federal government until 2023 will allow 16,000 non-seasonal foreign workers to apply for permanent residency for themselves and their families, except in Quebec. Seasonal agricultural workers are therefore excluded from the program across the country. Having contributed to Quebec’s economy and society for nine years, Carlos hopes the government might one day give him the opportunity to obtain permanent residency in Canada, so he can have the same rights as Canadians.

My greatest wish is to see my children grow up safe and to offer them a prosperous future. After the pandemic, I hope things can change for us.” Is Quebec society ready to follow the model of Enice Toussaint, who lives happily with her grandchildren? “It’s a big bus that has to be turned around, and that’s not easy,” concludes geriatrics researcher Gina Bravo.
